newsitem.title: INDIA: India RBI chief wants greater central bank freedom.
newsitem.headline: India RBI chief wants greater central bank freedom.

text.p: India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), needs greater autonomy if it is to contain inflation, Tuesday's edition of the Business Standard daily quoted the RBI governor as saying.
"The central bank must have full operational freedom to achieve the objectives it has set for itself," RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan told Business Standard in an interview.
"Autonomy has many dimensions. To me the most important dimension relates to the conduct of monetary policy," he said.
Rangarajan said autonomy did not imply that the central bank was not accountable for its actions and policies.

"The question of autonomy should be viewed from the perspective of the independence to choose the objectives of monetary policy and the freedom to pursue these objectiveds through a set of appropriate instruments," he said.
In a separate interview with the Economic Times also appearing on Tuesday, Rangarajan said the central bank was confident of keeping M3 money suply growth within target.

The RBI has set a target of 15.0-15.5 percent growth rate target for M3 in 1997/98 (April-March). The latest figures from the central bank show M3 grew by 16.6 percent year-on-year for the fortnight ended June 6.
"We are very conscious of the fact that the order of increase in money supply should be kept under control, and we will take policy decisions to ensure that," Rangarajan told the Economic Times.
The RBI chief said open market operations will be undertaken, if required, to keep money supply growth within target.
He said the policy approach will be to let the government complete as much of its budgeted borrowings as possible in the first half of the financial year.

"At this time last year, the central government had borrowed 130 billion rupees; this year the figure stands at about 260 billion rupees. And half the (borrowing) programme is yet to be completed," Rangarajan said.
"Trying open market operations now would compete with that borrowing programme, so we are saving that for later, should money supply growth warrant such action," Rangarajan.
